newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S.-Russian Mir crew face hitch, train for repair.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-Russian Mir crew face hitch, train for repair.

text.p: The crippled Mir space station was coping with a new navigational problem on Thursday but mission control said the Russian-American crew were safe and were practising for a risky and complex repair operation.

Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov told Reuters there had been an unexplained malfunction in all the station's gyrodines -- devices that keep the solar panels lined up to the Sun to gain maximum power as Mir hurtles round in Earth orbit.

The result was that the cosmonauts had to fire their rocket engines to keep Mir lined up to the sun and avoid losing even more electrical power. The station suffered a similar vicious circle of power loss last week after the June 25 collision with an unmanned Progress cargo craft during a docking exercise.

Officials would neither confirm nor deny a newspaper report the nearly fatal collision, which punctured part of the station and deprived Mir of up to half its electric power, was caused by a serious oversight by commander Vasily Tsibliyev.

"Mir is on its set orbit, but we're having to fire the engines more often. All the gyrodines are malfunctioning," Krikalyov said of the latest problem. "It presents no danger either for the station or the cosmonauts as we have enough fuel. But it is unpleasant."

Another Progress cargo craft is due to blast off from the Baikonur cosmodrome on the Kazakh steppe on Saturday carrying vital repair supplies. It will take two days to reach Mir, where the crew are waiting in dark, hot discomfort.
The lack of power will present Tsibliyev with a particularly difficult docking problem with the Progress, officials say.

He and Russian flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, are now training for the complex and risky job of entering the narrow confines of the punctured Spektr module in bulky spacesuits to reconnect its solar panels to the main batteries.

During the work, planned for July 11 or 14, British-born NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, will take to the station's three-seater Soyuz escape capsule -- the cosmonauts' last resort to get back to Earth if their repair mission goes badly wrong.
"We understand there are risks in this operation," Krikalyov told reporters. "So we are looking at fallback options."

Most serious would be an inability to seal off the holed module from the main craft after the work, which involves feeding 10 severed power cables back through the airtight doorway of the module using a specially made piece of equipment.
"If the hatch does not close, the cosmonauts will go back to the Soyuz and wait for a decision. If a danger arises the crew could quickly return to Earth," Krikalyov said.
Another plan would involve moving the Soyuz escape capsule to another, more secure, docking port separated by more airlocks from the risky passageway between the main section and Spektr.
Cosmonauts working in a mock-up of Mir at Star City near Moscow have decided the operation is practicable although three or four of the 10 severed cables are hard to reach.
A calm-sounding Tsibliyev spoke to Mission Control on Thursday as the cosmonauts set about testing their spacesuits.
"We'd like recommendations from you as soon as possible about how we can work in such cramped conditions in spacesuits," he said. "We have loads of cable around here and lots of piping.

Russia's Sevodnya daily, quoting unidentified sources, said investigators found Tsibliyev, 43, caused the collision by not reprogramming Mir's computers for the fact that the Progress was carrying nearly a tonne overweight of waste during the docking.
"I cannot confirm or deny how far the crew were at fault," Krikalyov said.
The accident was the worst in Mir's 11-years in space. Only split second thinking in slamming the hatches saved the crew from suffocation as air hissed out of the punctured module.
After a series of other potentially fatal mishaps, it has led to calls in Washington for NASA to end cooperation with Mir, which is part of preparations for a new international station.
